item.title: Beck | Ride Lonesome Tour — Tue Oct 27, 8:00 PM — Durham Performing Arts Center (DPAC)
item.description:
Produced by Beck and Mixed by Nigel Godrich, the song "Ride Lonesome” evokes the beautiful and haunting sonic landscapes and textures of 2015 Album of the Year GRAMMY winner Morning Phase and its spiritual predecessor, 2002’s classic Sea Change—and features multiple musicians who played on those milestone releases. From the resonant acoustic guitar strains of its opening to the emotional peaks of its final chorus, this long-awaited new original composition is the first indication of a different yet familiar direction for Beck in the year ahead. Come hear this and other wonderful songs from this iconic musician.

item.title: FIP Seminar: From Photons to Patients: Translating Optical Innovation into Biophotonic Clinical Impact — Wed Oct 28, 12:00 PM — Wilkinson Building
item.description:
Biomedical engineering continues to present an expanding range of opportunities to deepen our fundamental understanding of biological systems and human physiology. Yet a persistent gap remains between scientific discovery and its translation into technologies that meaningfully improve clinical care. My experience developing biomedical technologies and contributing to 16 issued U.S. patents has reinforced a central lesson: achieving meaningful impact often requires scientists and engineers to extend their work beyond fundamental discovery and embrace the scientific, technical, and translational risks associated with converting promising concepts into practical solutions.

item.title: MEMS Seminar: Seth Hutchinson, "Model-Based Methods in Today’s Data-Driven Robotics Landscape" — Wed Oct 28, 12:00 PM — Fitzpatrick Center Schiciano Auditorium Side A
item.description:
The Thomas Lord Department of Mechanical Engineering and Materials Science welcomes Professor Seth Hutchinson (Northeastern University) to deliver the MEMS Seminar, "Model-Based Methods in Today's Data-Driven Robotics Landscape."
ABSTRACT: Data-driven machine learning methods are making advances in many long-standing problems in robotics, including grasping, legged locomotion, perception, and more. There are, however, robotics applications for which data-driven methods are less effective. Data acquisition can be expensive, time consuming, or dangerous. Simulation methods also have limitations, particularly when complex dynamics require heavy computation and expose the so-called sim2real gap. Demonstration-based methods can fail when confronted with problems not represented in training examples, precluding provable performance guarantees.

item.title: Physics Colloquium - Revisiting Fusion’s Beginnings: A 1938 Mystery Meets a Modern Duke-Los Alamos Experiment — Wed Oct 28, 3:30 PM — None
item.description:
In 1938, Arthur Ruhlig at the University of Michigan reported an unexpected result while studying deuterium-deuterium fusion: evidence that tritium produced in one nuclear reaction could fuse with deuterium in a second. His brief Physical Review letter, now associated with the earliest observation of deuterium-tritium fusion, went unrecognized in the published literature for decades. Its rediscovery raised a question that could be tested experimentally: what would a modern recreation reveal?
This colloquium connects fusion's early history with a recent experiment by Duke's Triangle Universities Nuclear Laboratory and Los Alamos National Laboratory. Using modern neutron detection and complementary measurements, the team recreated the fusion reaction sequence, in agreement with modern calculations. item.title: Natasha Gordinsky: "Sonic Inheritance: War and Storytelling in Germanophone Post-Soviet Jewish Writing” — Wed Oct 28, 5:00 PM — Rubenstein Library Carpenter Conference Room 249
item.description:
The Sperling Center for Jewish Studies welcomes Natasha Gordinsky, who will give a lecture entitled "Sonic Inheritance: War and Storytelling in Germanophone Post-Soviet Jewish Writing." Gordinsky is a Senior Lecturer at the Department of Hebrew and Comparative Literature at the University of Haifa and is a member of the Israel Young Academy. Gordinsky received her PhD in Hebrew Literature from Hebrew University of Jerusalem in 2010. From 2010 till 2012 she was a post-doctoral Fellow of Minerva Foundation at Simon Dubnow Institute for Jewish History and Culture. Gordinsky is an author of two books: Kanon und Diskurs: Über Literarisierung jüdischer Erfahrungswelten, V&R 2009 (together with Susanne Zepp) and In Three Landscapes: Lea Goldberg's Early Writings, Magnes University Press 2016, that was recently published in German translation under the title »Ein elend-schönes Land« : Gattung und Gedächtnis in Lea Goldbergs hebräischer Literatur, V&R 2018.
Source: Duke University

The Jewish Law Student Association and Jewish Life at Duke welcome Judge Roy K. Altman for a discussion of his recent New York Times bestselling book, "Israel on Trial: Examining the History, the Evidence, and the Law."
Judge Altman has served as a United States District Judge for the Southern District of Florida since 2019. A graduate of Yale Law School and a former editor of the Yale Law Journal, he is an award-winning writer and commentator.
Before taking the bench, Altman served as a decorated federal prosecutor trying complex cases involving international crime and human trafficking and twice received the Department of Justice's highest honor. He was also named Federal Prosecutor of the Year. In April 2026, Altman published "Israel on Trial: Examining the History, the Evidence, and the Law," where he uses courtroom-style legal analysis to examine key claims made against Israel.

item.title: Roots Run Both Ways: A Filmmaker's Return and the Music That Never Left — Wed Oct 28, 6:30 PM — Center for Documentary Studies
item.description:
Join award-winning filmmaker and educator Jacqueline L. Olive, the 2026-28 Lehman Brady Joint Visiting Associate Professor of American Studies and Documentary Studies at Duke University and the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill, for an evening of conversation, music, and storytelling.
Olive will discuss her documentary filmmaking journey, her return to North Carolina, and the enduring influence of Black musical traditions on Americana music.
The evening begins with a conversation between Olive and filmmaker and Wake Forest University professor Peter Gilbert, followed by a discussion with Duke professor Mark Anthony Neal and acclaimed musician Leon Timbo about Olive's new oral history project "Roots & Reclamation" and her forthcoming documentary "African Americana."
A live musical performance by Timbo and an audience Q&A will conclude the program.
Weather permitting, the event will take place on the CDS front porch. In the event of rain, the program will move indoors.
